item.title: We Turned “Let Them” Into a Mantra But Skipped the Hard Part
item.description:
Emotion Regulation

We Turned “Let Them” Into a Mantra But Skipped the Hard Part

Here's what you need to know to truly "let them."

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • "Let them" is a great concept to help us notice our triggers and do something different.
  • Emotions make it hard to "let them."
  • Working with emotions in the body is key.

Mel Robbins' book Let Them is still a bestseller nearly two years after publication. The concept struck a chord with millions of people. This two-word phrase has become a mantra for navigating everything from disagreements to relationship breakdowns.

If someone doesn't invite you to their 50th birthday? Let them.

If your adult child makes choices you don't agree with? Let them.

If a friend ghosts you and pulls away? Let them.

“Let them” is like detaching with love. It’s taking your hands off the steering wheel of someone else’s life. The genius of "let them" is that it helps us notice something many of us do without realizing it: We try to control other people to feel better ourselves. The moment we recognize this tendency, we gain an opportunity to respond differently.

But this is just the first step.

Knowing we should "let them" doesn't necessarily make it easier to let go of our desire for people to change. If it were that easy, there would be far fewer controlling relationships, fewer codependent patterns, and far less emotional suffering.

So, in these circumstances, why is “let them” so hard? As an AEDP psychotherapist, I’d like to share a clinical example that you may relate to–even if you’re not in psychotherapy.

This story highlights the complexities of recognizing painful emotions and the brilliant ways we avoid them. How we respond to our complex emotional lives plays a significant role in our ability to find wisdom in the “let them” mindset.

Consider Sarah, a woman in her 50s whose daughter just graduated from high school. To celebrate her milestone, Sarah’s daughter left for a weeklong camping trip with her best friends. It’s the first time Sarah has let her daughter really “adult” and leave home without supervision.

Feeling a tad anxious, Sarah texts her daughter and says, “Remember to be careful. And did you take the bug spray and food I bought for you?” But she doesn't hear back from her.

Her mind starts spinning.

“Why isn't she responding?”

“Is she upset with me?”

“Is this what it’s going to be like when she goes to college?”

Sarah knows the "let them" philosophy. She tells herself, "She's doing her own thing. Let her live her life."

Despite her best efforts, however, she keeps checking her phone. Her compulsion is reminiscent of waiting by her landline for her crush to call during high school. When Sarah’s daughter doesn’t text back after 2 minutes, she fervently drafts a text, “Let me know if you’re still alive!”

Thankfully, she recognizes her own histrionics and doesn’t push send.

What's happening? From the outside, it looks like Sarah is an overprotective parent with a control problem. But beneath her urge for control lies something deeper.

The need to control others or a situation is a “defense mechanism.” Many of us associate “defense mechanisms” with Freud, discarding them as outdated psychobabble that holds no relevance today.

Defenses, however, are not nonsense. They are the brilliant ways we protect ourselves from what emotion researchers, such as psychologist Diana Fosha, who developed AEDP therapy, call “core emotions.”

These emotions are body-based programs that evolved for survival and so humans could thrive, just like thirst and hunger. What most people still haven’t learned is that these emotions are not under conscious control.

Core emotions prompt us to take actions that benefit us. A good example is fear. If a bear crossed your path, you’d immediately start running. Fear is the program that prompts the body to run.

When our core emotions are not validated, starting in childhood, we learn to bury or suppress them. And this was what was happening for Sarah.

Underlying Sarah’s deep need to control her daughter was fear: fear of being forgotten, fear of losing connection, and fear of abandonment. There was also sadness: sadness about her impending empty nest and her daughter needing her less. And let’s not forget about anger. Part of Sarah resented how much she had sacrificed and how little appreciation she received in return. In one of her unsent text drafts, Sarah said, “You’re so ungrateful! You won’t answer me. I feel so disrespected!” Sarah’s core emotions were not created by the present moment alone. They were amplified by her earlier attachment experiences.

Sarah grew up feeling unseen, unimportant, and emotionally alone. Whenever she felt sad, angry, or afraid, her parents accused her of being “overly sensitive.” Whenever she cried, her father called her a “drama queen” or a “crybaby.” These shaming words left Sarah feeling alone. Yet as a child, she relied on her parents for her care and survival. And so Sarah did what we all do when we’re left alone with our emotions: she learned to bury them and manage them with protective defenses.

Even though Sarah loves the “let them” theory, the problem isn’t that she hasn’t learned the right cognitive strategy; Sarah’s nervous system was sounding an alarm.

In my work as an AEDP psychotherapist, I teach a tool called the Change Triangle, which maps how emotions operate in the mind and body.

The Change Triangle is emotions 101. It’s the basic emotions education we all need, but few of us get.

Sarah's Change Triangle
Source: Hilary Jacobs Hendel

At the bottom of the triangle are our core emotions—fear, sadness, anger, joy, excitement, and disgust. Above them are inhibitory emotions such as anxiety, shame, and guilt. At the top are defenses: the automatic strategies we use to avoid emotional discomfort. Examples include overthinking, worrying, people-pleasing, criticizing, controlling, and obsessing. (Not to mention addiction and depression.)

These defenses are not character flaws. They are attempts to manage emotional pain. When Sarah struggled to “let” her daughter have her freedom, she was caught in a defense.

As Sarah slowed down, she noticed tightness in her chest, a lump in her throat, and a sinking feeling in her stomach. Instead of trying to outsmart her distress, she began to acknowledge her emotions. “Of course, I'm sad.” My daughter is leaving soon for college, she reminded herself.

“Of course, I'm scared.” I fear losing our deep connection, and my daughter’s silence highlights this fear.

“Of course, I’m angry.” My daughter didn’t respond, and her silence felt like an attack, a dagger to my heart.

When emotions are named, validated, and experienced in the body, something remarkable happens. The nervous system begins to settle. The emotional energy moves through rather than remaining stuck.

Only then does "let them" become more than a slogan. It becomes a possible choice.

The phrase "let them" helps us identify our impulse to control. This is brilliant. Emotional freedom, however, requires another step. To stop the impulse to control others, we must feel the emotions our defenses try to protect us from. In other words, before we can truly “let them,” we need to feel the emotions that exist deep within us.

Sarah realized that her daughter’s need for independence was not a rejection. It was a healthy and normal part of becoming an adult. Sarah’s ability to fully see her daughter deepened their relationship. Their conversations became more authentic, enjoyable, and loving.

"Let them" is a powerful beginning. An education in emotions helps us complete the journey.

item.title: Can Your Social Network Shape Your Economic Future?
item.description:
Friends

Can Your Social Network Shape Your Economic Future?

The importance of cross-class friendships for economic mobility.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Income inequality is high in the U.S., and people tend to have friends with similar socioeconomic status.
  • Social relationships are an important driver of educational and occupational success.
  • A recent study found that cross-class friendships strongly support economic mobility.

Social connections are the lifeblood of what it means to be human. Relationships are an integral part—if not the integral part—of the human experience. We know this is true for our personal lives; our romantic partners, kids, parents, and best friends are tremendous sources of happiness. But how important are relationships, and friendships specifically, for our professional lives?

The Importance of Cross-Class Friendships for Career Success

As it turns out, friendships are valuable sources of career capital. In one of the most thorough research investigations on the relationship between friendship and occupational success, a team of researchers examined a variety of social and economic variables from 21 billion friendship formations on Facebook among over 70 million adults in order to understand how friendships shape future income prospects and economic mobility in the United States.1 The U.S. has one of (if not the) highest rates of income inequality among all post-industrialized G7 nations, so this provides a fruitful arena to study.

The results were profound: Having economic cross-class friendships was vital to future income.

Typically, American friendships are strongly divided by socioeconomic status. Those from high socioeconomic status backgrounds tend to befriend others from similar backgrounds, while those from low SES backgrounds tend to befriend fellow people from low SES circumstances. This pattern, which has been dubbed homophily, is a common psychological finding: In essence, birds of a feather flock together in a wide range of domains.

In this study, researchers showed that those from the bottom 50 percent of the income distribution only had a small share of friends (38.8 percent) who were above the 50th percentile of the economic distribution. Yet the authors also found that intraclass friendships were crucial to future economic success, particularly amongst lower-income people. Cross-class friendship was a significant and positive correlate of upward mobility, meaning people with richer friends had better economic outcomes themselves.

The relationship between cross class friendships and income existed in a variety of different ZIP codes in the US, suggesting it was not just an artifact of a single state or city. However, certain locations displayed this dynamic more strongly than others.

Minneapolis, for example, has a larger share of low socioeconomic residents in comparison to Indianapolis, yet people in Minneapolis appear to have substantially more cross-class friendships. Children who grew up in low-income families in Minneapolis went on to have higher incomes ($34,300 at age 35 in 2015) in comparison to children from low-income families in Indianapolis ($24,700 at age 35 in 2015). A $10,000 income difference at age 35 is not trivial, and it was significantly predicted by cross-class friendships even more so than alternative metrics of social cohesion (how tight knit one’s social circle is) and civic engagement (e.g., volunteering).

Why Might Our Friends' Socioeconomic Status Influence Our Own?

So why does having friends from higher socioeconomic circumstances raise your own income? The best explanation may be that befriending higher SES people affords intellectual network capital. In other words, wealthier friends tend to come with increased access to information—perhaps about the best universities to attend, the best internships to acquire, or the best jobs to apply for.

Social networks tend to be information-rich in ways that can pay off directly or indirectly. For instance, research suggests that of all jobs, approximately 20 percent are achieved through cold applications, 20 percent are achieved through close ties (i.e., family members, romantic partners), and a resounding 60 percent are achieved through weak ties (i.e., colleagues, acquaintances, or friends).

The Biggest Takeaway: Institutions Can Help Foster Cross-Class Friendships

It would be too simplistic to conclude that lower-income people should strategically collect wealthier contacts. Friendship is reciprocal, not a transaction—and besides, the burden of crossing class boundaries should not fall only on the people with fewer resources.

The broader lesson, I argue, is institutional. Schools, workplaces, and community organizations can create repeated opportunities for people from different backgrounds to collaborate, talk, and build trust rather than merely occupy the same space, in addition to underscoring the importance of existing programs (e.g., Big Brother/Big Sister programs).

Networking may make many of us cringe—guilty as charged—but the deepest insight here is not that who you know replaces what you know; it is that knowledge and opportunity often move through human relationships. Diversity can put people in the same room—but only real connection determines whether they actually learn from and support one another.

item.title: Vigilant, Not Cynical: Staying Ethical Amid Dirty Tactics
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Vigilant, Not Cynical: Staying Ethical Amid Dirty Tactics

Staying ethical in a world of rule‑breakers.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Ethical behavior is not weakness; it can be a source of clarity and effectiveness.
  • Cynicism shuts people down, while vigilance helps them recognize and resist unethical tactics.
  • Understanding influence helps you resist manipulation without imitating it.

Every semester, in my Power and Influence course, a familiar moment arrives. We are deep into a negotiation exercise or a role‑play designed to surface real organizational dynamics, when a student raises a hand and says something like this:

“I am all for ethics, but I am tired of being victimized by people who are not.”

The room always goes quiet. Heads nod. Nearly everyone has felt this in some part of their life. They have watched people who bend rules, manipulate narratives, or weaponize relationships rise faster than those who try to do things the right way. They have seen unethical behavior rewarded. And they are frustrated.

I do not dismiss that frustration. I validate it. They are not imagining it. Unethical power exists. Unethical influence exists. And yes, sometimes unethical tactics work. They work more often than any of us would like to admit, and sometimes they work for a very long time. Acknowledging that reality is part of teaching power honestly.

Cynicism shuts people down. Vigilance wakes them up. Cynicism assumes that everyone is corrupt and that nothing can be done. Vigilance recognizes corruption when it appears and helps you protect yourself. Cynicism dismisses ethics as pointless. Vigilance treats ethics as a source of clarity and effectiveness. The difference between the two shapes how people navigate power.

This distinction is the foundation of how I teach the realities of power and influence.

The Mantra for Power and Influence

Years ago, I wrote a Psychology Today post introducing what I call the Mantra for Power and Influence. It goes like this:

“Don’t say or do what you feel like saying or doing. Say or do what’s effective.”

It sounds simple, but it’s not. It requires two skills that most people struggle with: self‑awareness and self‑regulation.

Self‑awareness means consciously noticing your emotional state instead of reacting on autopilot. Most people know they are angry or defensive, but they know it in a vague, background way. They do not pause long enough to recognize the emotion clearly. When you take even a moment to acknowledge what you are feeling, you interrupt the automatic pattern that leads to impulsive reactions.

Self‑regulation is the next step. It is the ability to resist the urge to say or do whatever your emotion is pushing you toward. If you feel like snapping at someone, you do not. If you feel like making a sarcastic remark, you do not. If you feel like shutting down, you do not. This is difficult, and nobody gets it right every time, but learning to do it more often is one of the most valuable skills you can develop.

This is not about being fake. It is about being effective. People can act strategically without crossing into manipulation. They can influence others without slipping into predatory behavior. They can exercise power without abandoning their character. Ethical effectiveness is still effectiveness, and it is often more durable.

The Misunderstood Machiavelli

This is also where I need to be clear about my relationship to Machiavelli. I assign The Prince in my course because it remains one of the most influential works ever written on power, and because its insights into human behavior still matter. But many people read Machiavelli superficially and come away with the cartoon version: the ruthless operator who endorses deception and cruelty. Some even act on that caricature. My Mantra for Power and Influence is not drawn from Machiavelli, and it is certainly not an endorsement of that distorted reading. The overlap is limited to one idea: regulating impulses so that emotion does not sabotage effectiveness. My approach is grounded in ethics, psychology, and communication science. Machiavelli’s writing was grounded in political survival. They intersect briefly, but they are not the same road.

Why Unethical Behavior Sometimes Works

Students often ask why unethical people sometimes rise to power. It is a fair question, and it deserves a fair answer. The truth is that unethical tactics can work. Anyone who has spent time in an organization has seen this firsthand. Pretending otherwise does not help students. Acknowledging it does. Many people assume that unethical behavior must eventually collapse, but that assumption reflects the comforting belief that the world is fair. It isn’t. And believing it only makes people more vulnerable.

But acknowledging it does not mean endorsing it. It simply means we are being honest about the world they are entering. Unethical behavior can produce results, but those results tend to be short‑term or situational. They come with costs that accumulate over time. Machiavelli, who is so often caricatured as the patron saint of ruthlessness, actually warned leaders to avoid hatred because hatred is fatal. That is not the advice of a villain. That is the advice of someone who understood human nature and the long arc of consequences.

This is why I tell students that the goal is not cynicism. Cynicism leads nowhere. It convinces people that corruption is universal and that their choices no longer matter. Vigilance works differently. It helps people recognize unethical tactics before those tactics harm them. Vigilance sharpens judgment. Cynicism dulls it. Vigilance keeps people engaged and effective. Cynicism leaves them stuck.

And vigilance requires knowledge. You cannot defend yourself against tactics you do not understand. This is why I teach Cialdini’s work on influence. His research explains how people respond to certain kinds of communication and behavior, and why those responses can be so powerful. These approaches are amoral. They can be used ethically or unethically. My goal is to help students recognize when those tools are being used against them and to help them use the same tools ethically and effectively. When I teach Cialdini, I emphasize both sides of the coin.

One of the biggest misconceptions students bring into the classroom is the belief that ethical behavior requires passivity. It does not. Ethical leaders can be assertive, strategic, and decisive. They set boundaries. They build coalitions. They persuade and influence. Ethics is not the opposite of power. Ethics is what makes power sustainable.

In the exercises I run, students see both worlds play out in real time. They see how ethical influence builds trust and stability. They also see how unethical influence can produce results that are sometimes quick and sometimes lasting, which is precisely why the temptation exists. They feel the tension between the two approaches. They feel the pull toward tactics they know are wrong. And in the debrief, we talk about how to navigate that tension without losing their integrity. It is not a warning that unethical behavior will inevitably collapse. It is a reminder that character and reputation matter, even when unethical people sometimes succeed.

Ethical power takes longer to build, but once it is built, it carries a kind of stability that shortcuts can never match. Unethical power often moves quickly, and sometimes it lasts longer than it should, which is exactly why people feel tempted by it. The real question is not whether unethical behavior sometimes succeeds. It does. The question is what kind of person you want to be while navigating power, and what kind of reputation you want to carry with you. Understanding unethical tactics helps you defend yourself, not imitate them. You do not need to abandon ethics to gain influence. You need to combine ethics with strategy. And in the end, the same principle still applies: do not say or do what you feel like saying or doing. Say or do what is effective and ethical.

item.title: The Costs and Benefits of Comparing Oneself
item.description:
Social Comparison Theory

The Costs and Benefits of Comparing Oneself

Social comparison can affect us positively or negatively.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Comparing ourselves with others in different ways is natural.
  • At work, comparisons may result in perceptions of unfairness.
  • Unfairness creates stress for which there are actions we can take to resolve.
Source: geralt/Pixabay

We compare ourselves with other people. We do so in different ways, in different situations. We may or may not be aware of the comparisons we make. We may or may not realize, for good or ill, how these comparisons affect our behaviors and our mental health. Do you compare yourself with a sibling, a friend, a parent, a co-worker, or your younger self? Over 70 years ago, the social psychologist Leon Festinger published his now-famous theory about social comparisons.

In my experience, one of the most practical and useful elaborations of Festinger’s work is J. Stacy Adams’s equity theory of motivation. Although originally applied primarily to issues of fairness in the workplace, equity theory can be useful in other situations. It can help us understand ourselves—and even motivate our behavior.

We can compare ourselves with another person or several people. We can also compare ourselves with a younger self or ourselves in a previous situation. For example, I might compare the benefits of my current job with the benefits I had in a previous job. Adams would say that I am comparing "outcomes." I would also be comparing what I bring to the job, such as my level of effort, knowledge, or inputs. Another person, other people, or ourselves at another time; each of these is what Adams called a referent. We compare our inputs and outcomes with those of referents. If they are different, we may see tension that sometimes can lead to stress.

For example, perhaps my referent is a co-worker. I perceive the co-worker as not working as hard as I do (inputs), yet I perceive him receiving more rewards (outcomes), such as higher pay or a promotion. I think this is not fair. I work harder, produce more, but I make less money and receive less recognition than this co-worker, who I perceive as working less yet has better pay and recognition. This perceived unfairness creates stress.

What can we do to reduce that stress? According to equity theory, we can:

  • Change our inputs: “Perhaps I need to work harder, smarter.”
  • Change our outcomes: “Boss, let’s talk about my contributions to our mission—and my pay.”
  • Change how we think about the situation: “Perhaps I don’t work as hard as I think I do.”
  • Change referent(s): “You know, I am more successful around here than Joe.”
  • Leave: “I think I’ll be happier in my new job.”

If both you and your referent have low inputs and low outcomes or high inputs and high outcomes, no tension should be created. However, if you have low inputs and high outcomes and your co-worker has high inputs and low outcomes, you might have some tension.

How we see others and ourselves is at the heart of equity theory, and there can be significant individual differences. Some people may be very concerned about clothing they wear vis-à-vis what clothing others wear, while others do not care. Some people are concerned about how much money they make, while for others, this is not a concern. The basis of the comparison can vary widely.

Our perceptions of others may be right or wrong. It is easy to assume others value what we value, the same outcomes, the same rewards. However, a co-worker may value job satisfaction or freedom to work from home over pay. Even if we compare ourselves in a previous job, or our younger years, there may be memory errors.

I would venture that most of us have multiple referents in our different roles or aspects of our lives. I have known people who made themselves miserable comparing themselves with a sibling, a friend, or a parent—people who otherwise should have been very happy. On the other hand, a referent may be an inspiration. A disadvantaged youth who looks up to an astronaut, musician, or athlete and learns that person had a disadvantaged youth. "If that person did it, I can do it." Thinking about the referents in your life might be a useful exercise.

item.title: When Regret Finds Its Voice
item.description:
Forgiveness

When Regret Finds Its Voice

How one father's apology opened the door to healing, forgiveness, and renewal.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Relationships begin to change only when acknowledged regret is translated into honest conversation.
  • When fathers apologize with sincerity, a bridge towards better connections with their adult children is built.
  • The path to family reconciliation is not paved with certainty, but with candor and heartfelt accountability.
Source: Ploscar/Pixabay

In my previous post, I wrote about my client Dennis’s painful memories of his incendiary response to a crisis that his son, Luke, was in the midst of during high school. We used a series of questions to spark a transformation of those memories into an opportunity for insight, growth, and a healthier relationship with his now college-bound son.

However, while self-awareness is an important step on the pathway towards healing, other steps deserve to be taken as well. Self-awareness by itself does not improve relationships—but acting on that self-awareness can.

To set that process into motion, Dennis agreed with me that it was time to revisit with Luke that harrowing time and see what they could accomplish together. With this in mind, they conjointly met with me in my office in an effort to piece things together. Our conversation went something like this:

Dennis: "I wanted to use our time together to talk about something I still feel very bad about."

Luke: "Which is?"

D: "My reaction when we got the call from the school about your selling Adderall to other students."

L: "Dad… that’s in the past. We don’t need to go over that."

D: "I know it’s in the past, and I know that you got past it, that we all got past it. But it still haunts me. I still feel bad about it."

Silence

Dr. Sachs (me): "What are you thinking, Luke?"

L: "I’m thinking that I still feel very embarrassed about what happened, too. It was a dumb thing to do, and I don’t know what was going through my head. I still can’t believe I did that."

D: I guess that’s part of why I feel bad, Luke. Instead of helping you figure out what was going through your head, I just blew up at you. And I said some terrible things. I just wanted you to stop doing what you were doing—but I wasn’t doing anything to help you figure out why you were doing what you were doing. That’s not being a very good father."

L: "Well, I wasn’t being a very good son."

D: "I know. But that’s not an excuse for me to treat you like I did. And I want to apologize."

L: "I feel like I should apologize, too."

D: "But let’s start with my apology. I’m very sorry for acting the way I did. In my conversations with Dr. Sachs, I’ve realized that there was a lot of fear behind my anger—fear about who you were becoming, fear about what you were doing, fear that you were going to be like your Uncle Will. And I let my fear overwhelm me—it turned into rage, and I turned that rage against you. I’m still disappointed in myself."

Silence

Dr. S.: "What are you thinking, Luke?"

Luke: (tearful) "I’m thinking that I’m disappointed in myself, too. I disappointed you and Mom, and I made everybody worry about me, and I hated myself for that. I guess I still do…"

Silence

Dr. S.: "Dennis, what do you want to say to Luke?"

D: (tearful) "That I love you. That I lost it. That I didn’t mean the things I said. That I love you so much and was afraid you were going to wind up in jail and I was going to lose you. I didn’t know how much terror was beneath my anger at you and I let it get the best of me."

L: "I know you love me, Dad. And I was pretty terrified back then, too. I was a terrible student, the Adderall wasn’t helping, anyway, and I figured I might as well sell a few and make some money, since it wasn’t doing me any good."

D: "I shouldn’t have blown up."

L: "I don’t know, Dad. Maybe you needed to."

D: "No, I didn’t. Maybe I needed to actually sit down and talk with you and try to understand you, rather than terrorize you."

Silence

L: (very softly) "I guess that would have helped."

D: "I should have been there for you then. I am trying to be here for you now."

L: "I know, Dad, I know."

Dennis, Luke, and I then spent some time discussing their shared tendency to respond to their mistakes with self-hatred, rather than self-examination.

Their touching conversation demonstrates how relational wounds from the past can be healed in the present when regret is experienced, rather than repressed, which opens the door to self-acceptance rather than self-punishment.

Sometimes, growth is more likely to come about not from having perfect answers, but from asking, and reflecting upon, better questions.

item.title: Unclear Job Expectations Are a Clear Recipe for Problems
item.description:
Workplace Dynamics

Unclear Job Expectations Are a Clear Recipe for Problems

Employees need to know what is expected of them.

Posted July 27, 2026

Key points
  • Lack of clarity is a major enemy of job satisfaction.
  • Both manager and employee need to have a shared understanding of what constitutes excellent performance.
  • If shared expectations are well-created at the outset, the back-end evaluation can be more straightforward.

I was recently speaking with someone about her experience as an employee for a large organization in the corporate world. Her main memory was that it was confusing and she never really knew what was expected of her.

Role ambiguity is a common, frustrating situation.
Source: Yan Krukau / Pexels

Even though her management thought highly of her, she didn't like the job; she found it stressful and ended up leaving that environment and choosing to do a more physical type of work—where at least there was no uncertainty about what the job entailed.

Enemy of Satisfaction

This story isn't unusual. Lack of clarity is a major enemy of job satisfaction.

Ample research examines this workplace phenomenon. One study that analyzed six decades of research concluded that role ambiguity "tends to be the most detrimental driver of employee and organizational outcomes" when compared with role conflict and role overload.

Another study addressing job expectations from a different perspective found that only 14 percent of employees felt strongly that "their performance reviews inspire them to improve," and in fact could "actually make performance worse."

In short, when employees are unsure what's expected of them and how they're being evaluated on it, it's a fair bet they won't be happy with an organization and in all likelihood won't do their best work for it.

Metrics Matter

I had the good fortune early in my management career to become friends with some very capable HR folks who drummed into me the importance of making it crystal clear to direct reports exactly what I (and the organization) was expecting from them, and how their performance would be assessed.

At that time we used what was called a SMART employee evaluation system. There are numerous different ways this acronym can be interpreted, but as a manager my favorite was the following—the first letters signified that an employee's goals should be:

  • Specific
  • Measurable
  • Agreed-upon
  • Reasonable
  • Time-bound.

Some of these parameters are self-evident. To take a simple example, it's obviously not a clear goal to say that Josephine "is expected to be good at making widgets." How does one define good? It's a vague term. Whereas it's much clearer to say that Josephine "is expected to make 20 high-quality widgets each hour."

But the element of this rubric that I always felt was both most important and undervalued was the deceptively simple phrase agreed-upon.

Skin in the Game

The job of management becomes a whole lot easier when both manager and employee have a shared common understanding of what constitutes excellent performance. To this end, I spent a great deal (some might say an obsessive amount) of time with an employee discussing goals, articulating them, quantifying them, and communicating back and forth to determine what success in a given year really looked like. We might easily have three or four drafts of a document before we ended up with something we both felt worked.

I always believed it was time well spent. It also made life a whole lot easier at the end of the year when it came time to do employee evaluations. If the shared expectations were well and thoughtfully created at the outset, the back-end evaluation was generally a straightforward process.

Management isn't an easy job; anyone who says it is probably hasn't managed a whole lot of people. I used to say I made so many mistakes in my management career that I could no longer remember the first couple hundred. But being complicit in unclear job expectations wasn't one of them.
